image_description: A collection of vintage and antique smoothing irons displayed on dark wooden shelves against a white wall. The image features multiple instances: two heavy cast-iron sad irons on the top left, a green-painted charcoal or alcohol iron in the center, a flat-top electric iron with a wooden handle on the right, and a smaller nickel-plated electric iron on the bottom shelf. The objects exhibit varying degrees of metallic reflection and historical design styles.

checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The proportions relative to the shelving and handles suggest standard hand-held appliance dimensions.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Ergonomic handle on top of molded body.

checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: Vintage sad irons do not have steam holes. The angle and resolution of the electric irons prevent verification of soleplate perforations.

checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: Black power cords are clearly visible extending from the rear of the electric irons on the top right and bottom shelf.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Pointed tip for precision ironing around buttons and collars.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The pointed tips are a defining feature of the visible sad irons and are present on the electric models.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Polished stainless steel or non-stick coated aluminum soleplate.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The metallic surfaces show appropriate reflectivity and texture for polished steel or nickel plating, consistent with vintage appliances.
The bodies appear to be cast iron (sad irons) or molded metal/plastic composites (electric irons), fitting the material description.

The metal support bracket under the bottom shelf has a slightly soft, undefined geometry where it connects to the wall, lacking sharp mechanical edges.
The alignment of the two sad irons is slightly unnatural; the rear iron's handle seems to float slightly above the body without a clear connection point due to occlusion/shadow ambiguity.

selected_experts.reason: To confirm the specific sub-types of irons (sad iron, electric iron) and ensure they are correctly identified as household appliances rather than abstract shapes.
To verify the physical contact points between the heavy irons and the shelves, ensuring no floating objects or impossible gravity-defying placements.

To analyze the consistency of specular highlights on the metallic surfaces, ensuring they match a single light source environment.

Physical contact shadows between irons and shelves
Consistency of metallic reflections across different materials
